front: Name two positive impacts of websites on businesses.
back:
1) Global reach — customers anywhere can find and buy from the business.
2) 24/7 availability — customers can browse/buy at any time without staff present.

front: What is the 'digital divide'?
back: The gap between people who have good access to the internet/digital devices/skills and those who do not, which websites can widen if not designed inclusively.

front: Which law covers how a website must handle users' personal data?
back: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 — they set rules on collecting, storing, using and protecting personal data.

front: What does the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protect against on websites?
back: Copying someone else's text, images, video or other creative work without permission or credit.

front: What is 'alt text' and why does it matter?
back: A short text description added to an tag. Screen readers announce it to visually impaired users, and it displays if the image fails to load.

front: Give two features of an accessible website.
back:
1) Good colour contrast between text and background.
2) Text that can be resized without breaking the layout (and works with screen readers).

front: What key things should a client brief define?
back: Purpose of the site, target audience, required content/features, branding/style requirements, and any technical constraints.

front: What is a sitemap?
back: A diagram showing the pages of a website and how they connect/link to each other — used to plan navigation and structure before building.

front: What is a wireframe?
back: A simple, low-detail sketch/diagram showing where content and features will be placed on a page — layout only, not final colours/fonts.

front: What is 'house style'?
back: The consistent visual identity of a website/brand — same colours, fonts, logo placement and tone of writing used across every page.

front: What is HTML used for?
back: HyperText Markup Language defines the STRUCTURE and content of a web page (headings, paragraphs, images, links, etc.).

front: Name three semantic HTML5 elements.
back: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <article>, <section>, <footer> (any three) — these describe the meaning of content, not just its appearance.

front: What is CSS used for?
back: Cascading Style Sheets control the PRESENTATION of a web page — colours, fonts, spacing, layout, and responsiveness.

front: What is the CSS Box Model made up of?
back: Content → Padding → Border → Margin (from the inside out).

front: What is a media query used for?
back: Applying different CSS rules depending on screen size/device — the basis of responsive web design.

front: What is JavaScript used for on a website?
back: Adding INTERACTIVITY and dynamic behaviour — form validation, responding to clicks, updating content without reloading the page.

front: What is the difference between a code editor and a WYSIWYG tool?
back: A code editor (e.g. VS Code) shows raw code you write yourself. A WYSIWYG tool (e.g. Dreamweaver Design view) lets you build visually and generates the code for you.

front: When should you use JPEG vs PNG for images?
back: JPEG: photographs (good compression, no transparency). PNG: logos/icons/graphics needing transparency or sharp edges.

front: What is a CMS and give one example.
back: A Content Management System lets you create/edit website content through an interface without coding every page by hand. Example: WordPress.

front: Name four types of website testing.
back: Functional testing, usability testing, accessibility testing, cross-browser/device testing (also: performance testing).

front: What is minification?
back: Removing unnecessary characters (spaces, line breaks, comments) from CSS/JS/HTML files to reduce file size and improve load speed.

front: What two things do you need to publish a website live on the internet?
back: A domain name (the web address) and web hosting (server space to store and serve the site's files).

front: What is the difference between a hierarchical and a linear sitemap?
back: Hierarchical: branches from a homepage into sections/sub-pages (tree structure). Linear: pages follow one after another in a fixed sequence (e.g. a step-by-step form).

front: What is the difference between an internal, external and inline stylesheet?
back: Inline: style attribute on one element. Internal: <style> block in the HTML head. External: separate .css file linked with <link> — best for reuse across pages.
